title: Word Embeddings
oneLineScope: Dense learned word vectors: word2vec and GloVe, and the analogy arithmetic that surprised everyone.
prose:
The count-and-factorize pipeline of the previous node works, but it is a two-stage affair: build a sparse PPMI matrix, then run SVD to compress it. The neural approach collapses those stages into one: train a shallow network whose sole purpose is to produce good word vectors, letting gradient descent discover the compression directly from the prediction objective. The resulting dense vectors — embeddings, meaning fixed-dimensional real-valued representations of discrete symbols — are the input representation that every subsequent architecture in this graph depends on. When we say a transformer “takes tokens as input,” what it actually receives is a lookup into an embedding matrix; this node is where that matrix comes from.

The embedding matrix

Before the architectures, the data structure. Fix a vocabulary of \(V\) word types. An embedding matrix \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}\) assigns each type a row vector of dimension \(d\). The integer index of a word (its position in the vocabulary) is used to select its row by lookup, so an embedding is simply a learned parameter table. The embedding dimension \(d\) is a hyperparameter, typically 100–300 for word2vec-era models. During training, gradient descent updates every row that is “looked up” in a given batch, leaving unmentioned rows unchanged. At the end of training, the rows are the word vectors.

word2vec: the prediction objective

Mikolov et al. (2013) introduced two shallow architectures under the word2vec umbrella. Both are motivated by the same idea: instead of counting co-occurrences and factorizing, directly train a network to predict which words tend to appear together, and harvest the word vectors from the weight matrices learned in that process.

CBOW (Continuous Bag of Words) predicts a center word from the average of its context word embeddings — a fast, smoothed model that works well for frequent words.

Skip-gram reverses the direction: given a center word \(w_{\text{center}}\), predict each of the surrounding context words \(w_{\text{ctx}}\) within a window of size \(m\). The training objective is to maximize the log-likelihood over all \((\text{center, context})\) pairs in the corpus:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \sum_{\text{pairs}} \log p(w_{\text{ctx}} \mid w_{\text{center}}) \]

where \(p(w_{\text{ctx}} \mid w_{\text{center}})\) is a softmax over the entire vocabulary \(V\):

\[ p(w_{\text{ctx}} \mid w_{\text{center}}) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \cdot \mathbf{e}'_{\text{ctx}})}{\sum_{v=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \cdot \mathbf{e}'_v)} \]

Here \(\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the row of the input embedding matrix \(E\) for the center word, and \(\mathbf{e}'_{\text{ctx}} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the corresponding row of a second, output embedding matrix \(E' \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}\). Two separate matrices for input and output roles are standard; after training, the input matrix \(E\) is used as the word embeddings. The network has no hidden layer between these two matrices — it is deliberately shallow, which keeps training tractable at large vocabulary sizes.

Negative sampling

The full-vocabulary softmax in the denominator above requires summing over \(V\) terms for every training example — with \(V = 10^5\)–\(10^6\), this is prohibitive. The practical solution, introduced in Mikolov et al. (2013b), is negative sampling: replace the softmax with a binary discrimination problem. For each true \((\text{center, context})\) pair, sample \(k\) “negative” context words at random from a noise distribution (the unigram distribution raised to the \(3/4\) power, to undersample very frequent words). The objective becomes:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{NEG}} = \log \sigma(\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \cdot \mathbf{e}'_{\text{ctx}}) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}_{w_i \sim P_n}\left[ \log \sigma(-\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \cdot \mathbf{e}'_{w_i}) \right] \]

where \(\sigma\) is the logistic function and \(P_n\) is the noise distribution. You can recognize this as noise-contrastive estimation (NCE): the model learns to distinguish true co-occurrences from noise-generated ones, and the log-likelihood of the true pair relative to the noise pairs is maximized. The statistical framing is exact: NCE approximates the full softmax at a fraction of the computational cost, and with \(k = 5\)–\(20\) negatives it recovers nearly the same quality vectors. This is the practical trick that made word2vec fast enough to run on billions of tokens on a single machine.

GloVe: count-based, but still learned

Pennington, Socher, and Manning (2014) returned to the count-matrix perspective with GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation). Rather than predicting local context windows, GloVe trains on the global word–word co-occurrence matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times V}\) computed over the full corpus, where \(X_{ij}\) is the number of times word \(j\) appears in the context of word \(i\). The objective factorizes a function of these global counts:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{GloVe}} = \sum_{i,j=1}^{V} f(X_{ij}) \left( \mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}'_j + b_i + b'_j - \log X_{ij} \right)^2 \]

where \(f(X_{ij})\) is a weighting function that down-weights very common co-occurrences, \(b_i\) and \(b'_j\) are scalar bias terms, and the objective asks the dot product of the two embedding vectors to approximate the log co-occurrence count. The explicit connection back to Harris and the PPMI matrix of the previous node is deliberate: GloVe makes the factorization explicit and optimizes it directly with gradient descent rather than algebraic SVD.

Empirically, word2vec (predictive, local windows) and GloVe (count-based, global matrix) produce vectors of comparable quality on most benchmarks. The theoretical gap is smaller than the architectural difference suggests: Levy & Goldberg (2014) showed that skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix, so both methods are, at bottom, low-rank matrix factorizations of co-occurrence statistics, differing mainly in which statistics they privilege and how the optimization proceeds.

Analogy arithmetic

The result that caught everyone’s attention was not retrieval quality but geometry. Mikolov et al. observed that simple arithmetic on the learned vectors could recover semantic and syntactic relations. The most cited example:

\(\mathbf{e}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{e}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{e}_{\text{woman}} \approx \mathbf{e}_{\text{queen}}\)

The vector offset from man to king is approximately the same as the offset from woman to queen. Similar parallelograms emerge for capital–country relations (Paris − France + Italy ≈ Rome), verb tenses (walked − walk + swim ≈ swam), and comparative adjectives.

This is striking and real: the vectors genuinely encode relational structure that was nowhere explicitly stated in the training objective. The explanation is distributional. If “king” and “man” share all their masculine contexts and differ mainly in their regal contexts, and “queen” and “woman” share all their feminine contexts and differ in the same regal contexts, then their positions in the learned embedding space will reflect that structure as a parallel offset.

The honest caveat: the effect is sensitive to the specific word pairs, the training corpus, the dimensionality \(d\), and normalization choices. Accuracy on the standard analogy benchmark (Mikolov et al.’s Google analogy set) ranges from roughly 40% to 75% depending on these factors. Results are often cherry-picked in presentations; the phenomenon is real but should be understood as a statistical tendency, not a reliable algebraic identity. The later work of Linzen (2016) and others showed the effect can disappear for less canonical examples.

The fundamental limitation: static representations

Both word2vec and GloVe produce static embeddings: one fixed vector per word type, regardless of context. Bank in “river bank” and in “central bank” map to the same row of \(E\) at inference time. This is the same limitation we identified in LSA; the distributional hypothesis is satisfied in expectation over all contexts, but individual uses are not distinguished. The remedy requires making representations contextual — recomputing them from the token’s actual surroundings at each occurrence. That is precisely what attention does: scaled dot-product attention, the subject of node 06, is the mechanism by which a static embedding is transformed into a context-sensitive representation by attending to the rest of the sequence. Word embeddings are the starting point — the initial \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) fed to the transformer — and what comes out the other end of each attention layer is something much richer.

diagrams.caption: Skip-gram architecture: a center word is looked up in the V×d input embedding matrix, producing a d-dimensional vector that is scored against the output embedding matrix to predict context words. Negative sampling replaces the full-vocabulary softmax with k+1 binary logistic decisions.
diagrams.altText: A left-to-right pipeline. On the left, a box labeled center word (integer index) feeds into a box labeled input embedding matrix E, shape V by d, via an arrow labeled lookup. The lookup extracts a single row vector labeled e_center, shape 1 by d. That vector feeds into a box labeled output embedding matrix E-prime, shape V by d, via a multiply arrow, producing a score vector of shape 1 by V. A note reads: full softmax over V is intractable. An arrow leads to a box labeled negative sampling: 1 true context word plus k noise words, logistic loss. The output on the right is labeled updated embeddings.
diagrams.prompt: Structural data-flow diagram, left to right, of the skip-gram word2vec architecture with negative sampling. Start on the left with a small box labeled 'center word (index)'. An arrow labeled 'lookup' leads into a tall rectangle labeled 'E (input embeddings)' with shape annotation 'V × d'; a highlighted row is extracted from it, drawn as a thin rectangle labeled 'e_center' with shape '1 × d'. An arrow from e_center labeled '× E′ (output embeddings, V × d)' leads to a score vector of shape '1 × V'. Below the score vector, add a note: 'full softmax over V: intractable (V ≈ 10⁵)'. An arrow leads into a box labeled 'negative sampling' containing: '1 true context pair (logistic +)' and 'k noise-sampled words (logistic −)'. The final output on the right is labeled 'gradient → update E rows'. Label every matrix with its name and shape. Mark V × d on both E and E′. Keep it clean and structural.

diagrams.caption: Analogy arithmetic as parallel vector offsets: the offset from man to king is the same as the offset from woman to queen, illustrating that the embedding space encodes the gender–royalty relation as a consistent direction.
diagrams.altText: A 2-D coordinate space with four labeled points: man and woman in the lower region, king and queen in the upper region. Arrows connect man to king and woman to queen, both pointing in the same upper-right direction and labeled with the same offset delta. A dashed arrow from king minus man plus woman points to queen. A note reads: vector arithmetic recovers relational structure — but effect is sensitive to corpus and parameters.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual diagram showing word embedding analogy arithmetic as a parallelogram in 2-D space. Draw a 2-D coordinate space (axes lightly sketched, unlabeled). Place four labeled word points: 'man' (lower-left), 'woman' (lower-right), 'king' (upper-left), 'queen' (upper-right), arranged as the four corners of a rough parallelogram. Draw an arrow from man to king, labeled 'royalty offset'. Draw an arrow from woman to queen, labeled the same offset, both arrows parallel and approximately equal in length. Draw a dashed arrow from the tip of (king − man + woman) to queen, labeled 'king − man + woman ≈ queen'. Add a short margin note: 'offsets encode relations — but effect is corpus- and parameter-sensitive'. No equations beyond the label; this is the intuition diagram.

bibliography.citation: Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013). Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space. arXiv:1301.3781.
bibliography.annotation: The original word2vec paper. Introduces both CBOW and skip-gram architectures and reports the analogy evaluation results. §2 defines the models; §3 describes the training; §4.2 is the analogy task. The paper is short and worth reading directly.

bibliography.citation: Mikolov, T., Sutskever, I., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013). Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality. NeurIPS. arXiv:1310.4546.
bibliography.annotation: The negative-sampling paper. §2.2 introduces the negative-sampling objective and the noise distribution; §2.3 explains subsampling of frequent words. This is the practical version of word2vec most implementations actually use. The NCE connection is discussed in the appendix.

bibliography.citation: Pennington, J., Socher, R., & Manning, C. D. (2014). GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation. EMNLP.
bibliography.annotation: The GloVe paper. §2 derives the weighted least-squares objective from co-occurrence statistics; §3 justifies the log co-occurrence target. The comparison to skip-gram in §4 is useful for understanding where the two approaches converge and diverge.

Visual walk-through of the skip-gram training process, negative sampling, and the resulting embedding geometry. Complements the formal papers well; particularly useful for the intuition behind what the network is actually learning step by step.
